text:
I see this one making the rounds as some bearish takedown of AI and in particular neoclouds.

1. He’s right that standing these massive AI datacenters is extremely hard. 
2. Yes, capital is harder to come by and will present a challenge for some companies.
3. He’s not a disinterested third party providing a viewpoint. 

I own $SPCX and believe it may be the largest AI hyperscaler in the not too distant future. Amazing execution. I also have positions in $IREN and $CRWV. 

But, let’s not pretend that there is no self interest here. Crushing the NEOs is absolutely in the best interest of Elon and SpaceX here. Better for pricing power, capital allocation, margins, customer acquisition, and so on and so forth. 

Note SpaceX still plans to stand up 10s of GW in short order because it is really good business for the company. The less competition the better. 

So two things can be true at the same time. The conditions Elon speaks to are real, but creating a massive spiral for smaller AI clouds is definitely in his best interest. It’s good use of the platform and a good chess move. But it isn’t just some altruistic advice for investors. 

Carry on.

text:
Good observation on the dilution risks with $IREN. 

The dilution has been pretty bad looking backwards. It wouldn’t be that big of a concern if mgmt didn’t top themselves up for that dilution. It creates a fundamental misalignment between management and shareholders and reeks of poor corporate governance. 

The flip side of that coin is that the Roberts brothers will lose meaningful say in the company if they get diluted and we don’t want that either. These two are the visionaries behind the company and the engine behind its growth. If massively diluted, they either get distracted by other endeavours or other investors jump in and drive the governance from the boarded level. 

A catch 22. 

That is why, in specific circumstances like the one IREN is in, with a steep growth curve ahead of it, mgmt top-ups are a necessary evil. 

But, as a private markets investor, it’s a tough pill for me to swallow. 

As for $NUAI, it doesn’t fit in the same conversation as IREN just yet. NUAI is a different risk profile altogether until they sign a tenant.

All that said, both companies are dirt cheap. Do the napkin math on what a fully leased MW generates in revenue (under either business model) today vs the cost of create said revenue and you’ll find these investments very compelling. 

Overthink it and you miss the opportunity. 

NFA

BREAKING DOWN GOVERNMENT REVENUE ACROSS SPACE INDUSTRY

Government revenue across space industry puts into perspective which companies depend on federal budgets and which have built commercial businesses large enough to grow beyond them:

Tier 1: Defense Contractors
• $YSS 99%
• $FLY 95%
• $VOYG 85%
• $LUNR 80%
• $HAWK 80%

Tier 2: Anchored Hybrids
• $RDW 50%
• $RKLB ~46% (post Iridium pro forma)
• $BKSY 45%

Tier 3: Commercial Hybrids 
• $LYNX 35%
• $PL 25%
• $SPIR 25%

Tier 4: Commercial Platforms 
• $SPCX 17%
• $VSAT 15%
• $GILT 15%
• $MDA 5%

What's interesting is that SpaceX remains one of government's most important launch providers yet government contracts account for just 17% of revenue which tells you how large Starlink's commercial business has become with SpaceX's AI biz adding another growth engine beyond space.

And you can see Rocket Lab moving in a similar direction with its Iridium acquisition bringing in a much larger commercial subscriber base without giving up government biz that helped it scale in first place.

en_summary: FSD v15 is starting to hit cars today, and I think this is a really BIG one. Elon says wider release coming in December with holiday update, calling it something special. First wave. Tesla says 25x better handling of safety critical cases, release notes describe 25x improvement in critical intervention rate.
text:
FSD v15 is starting to hit cars today, and I think this is a really BIG one.

Elon says the wider release is coming in December with the holiday update, calling it “something special.” This is the first wave, so if your car hasn’t received it yet, that’s normal fyi. 

The number everyone’s going to talk about is 25x.

Tesla says it's “25x better handling of safety critical cases,” while the release notes describe a 25x improvement in the critical intervention rate... that’s about situations where a driver needs to step in for safety. 

Tesla upgraded the vision encoder, the part of the AI that makes sense of what the cameras see. It’s shared with Robotaxi and Optimus, and Tesla says it was trained on millions of internet videos to help it understand more situations and learn more efficiently. A core piece of how the car, the robotaxi and the robot understand the world is now shared.

Then there’s Tesla Reality View.

The familiar gray driving display is now being replaced by a detailed view of the world around the car, created live from a virtual viewpoint above it. Ashok says the same model that drives the car also draws that scene. Arrows show the turns FSD plans to make, and pins show where it wants to park. 

Elon says you can tap a point in that view to tell the car where to go, with turn markers floating overhead like a video game. 

He says, “It’s like GTA" and the new visualization uses less computing power than the old one.

Tesla also lists better detection of road

$MU $SNDK $SKHY Fair question, and the honest answer is: plenty, starting with this industry.

Micron itself, 2018. At the peak it traded at roughly 4 to 5x forward earnings, with gross margin at a filed 61% in Q4 of fiscal 2018, and the stock still lost about half into 2019 as earnings collapsed. ZIM, 2021 to 2022: near 1 to 2x peak earnings, enormous dividends paid out in cash, and still down roughly 80% from the peak when container rates normalized. US homebuilders in 2005: roughly 6 to 8x peak earnings, after which earnings went negative and the stocks fell 70% and more. Dry bulk shipping in 2007: low multiples on peak charter rates, then declines of 90% and more.

The common thread is not the multiple. It is that the earnings were spot-priced. When the spot price turned, the denominator vanished, and the low multiple turned out to be the market pricing that evaporation in advance. That base rate is exactly why memory trades at 2x and not 12x today.

Where this cycle differs is confined to the contracted share: multi-year agreements with minimum pricing, and 12.9B dollars of contract liabilities on Micron's balance sheet at fiscal 2026 year end per its 10-K, cash collected in advance. No name in the precedent set had that construction. The uncontracted share of memory earnings carries precisely the risk those names did, and contracts themselves can still be amended by mutual agreement, which is the channel to watch. December 17, and the first-quarter contract prints after

It keeps its Overweight rating and $300 price target, more than double the current price per share.

Morgan Stanley puts a full payload at 50 Tbps of gross capacity, of which 2.5 Tbps is salable. 

The step up from the current fleet is large:
- Each V3 satellite has about ten times the downlink capacity of the V2 Mini satellites flown on Falcon 9. 
- One Starship launch adds 20 to 25 times the bandwidth of a Falcon 9 launch, equal to two or three months of Falcon 9 Starlink flights. 
- SpaceX stopped flying Starlink missions on Falcon 9 from Florida in late August, leaving Vandenberg as its only Falcon 9 Starlink pad. 

Morgan Stanley also expects Starship to cut SpaceX's internal variable launch cost from about $1,000 per kilogram in 2026 to about $500 by 2030 and about $140 by 2040, and expects weekly Starship launches by the end of 2027. It notes that Starlink V4 is planned at roughly ten times the capacity of V3 again.

At about $140 the stock is 4% above its $135 offer price, while Morgan Stanley's 2027 and 2028 EPS estimates have risen 80% and 60% since early July. 

It calculates 17.5 times its own 2028 earnings and 11.2 times consensus, both excluding tax benefits, against 16 times for the S&P 500.

text:
博通和谷歌的目前合作关系挺有意思的，我把官方说过的话和市场传的消息放在一起理了一遍。

先说没变的。4月两家签了长期协议，博通继续为谷歌开发和供应未来几代TPU。6月陈福阳说谷歌给的是一笔数额非常大的金额承诺，没给数字。9月他又说，博通计划未来几年每年交付几百亿美元的TPU。

变了的是，博通不再是独家，这是它自己承认的。6月有分析师问到份额，陈福阳说：我们当然想拿下每一个设计，但谷歌需求涨得太快，我们完全预期他们会有多个来源。

另一个来源是联发科。供应链传得很凶，郭明錤说下一代v9和再下一代v10都由联发科独家设计，这周又说谷歌砍了明年100万颗博通做的8i。谷歌和博通都没回应。

但两家公司自己的说法没这么绝对。陈福阳9月说，2028、2029年谷歌的需求，会由"我们今天正在和谷歌一起开发的"后几代TPU来满足。

联发科10月的电话会上，管理层说它的第二代AI芯片2028年一季度量产，市场普遍认为这就是谷歌的v9，公司没有点名。有分析师问，到了这一代，你们会不会成为这家客户的主要供应商。财务长答的是：跟所谓的竞争项目比，对方性能差得很远。这等于承认了v9这一代是有竞争项目的。但目前我猜V9主力应该像外界说的给了联发科。

至于再下一代，也就是市场说的v10，蔡力行说定义还要时间才能定下来。谈到整体竞争时他说得很克制：对手很强，我们会赢下属于我们的那部分，说明当时还没定下来。

9月高盛科技大会上有一段问答很有意思。主持人问：投资者担心谷歌把越来越多的设计收回去自己做，你们的护城河在哪？陈福阳没有正面回答谷歌会不会这么做，讲的全是技术：高速接口、SerDes、多芯片集成、先进封装。然后说过去30年博通一直靠工程能力赢对手，这次也一样，不管对手是同行，还是，用他的原话，"更有意思的是"，客户自己。

把客户算进竞争对手，说明他很清楚谷歌在做什么。

我的理解是，合作的重心换了。核心计算单元谷歌可以自己设计，这部分博通守不住。值钱的地方挪到了怎么把多颗芯片拼成一颗、让它们高速通信，这正好是博通最强的。

这个判断对不对，下一代就是考试。联发科那款是多颗芯片拼的，封装换成了一家美国IDM的工艺，新伙伴、新制程、新封装一起上。联发科说进度正常，良率还在爬。顺利量产，顺利量产，说明这道护城河别人也跨得过去；

出问题，谷歌手里还有博通已经在量产的v8，以及博通正在开发的后续型号。

一句话概括现在的状态：钱还在，独家没了，下一代两家都在做。12月9日博通财报，看管理层怎么回应。

以上是个人思路，不构成投资建议。
